name: JWTs and Session Tokens
intent: Choose between an opaque session id looked up on every request and a signed, self-contained token any service can verify, and know exactly what each choice costs in revocation, lookups and attack surface.
scenario: An API made of many microservices (orders, billing, ...) must authenticate users. A user's access token is stolen by a script injected into the web app. How long can the thief keep calling the API, and how many auth lookups does the platform pay to find out?
problem: HTTP is stateless, so every request must carry proof of who is calling. A server-side session id is trivially revocable but forces a store lookup on every request in every service. A signed token (JWT, JSON Web Token) is verified locally with no lookup, but it is valid until it expires: you cannot take it back. Add the many ways to verify a JWT incorrectly (alg none, algorithm confusion, no audience check) and the choice is as much about operational risk as about performance.

howItWorks.title: Server-side session: an opaque id and a lookup
howItWorks.text: After login the server stores the session (user id, created, last seen, device) under a random id of at least 128 bits from a cryptographic random generator (CSPRNG) and sets it in a cookie such as __Host-sid with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax. Every request does a lookup in Redis or a database. Revocation is a delete: the next request fails. The price is a network round trip per request, and a store every service must reach or share.

howItWorks.title: JWT: header.payload.signature, verified locally
howItWorks.text: A JWT is three base64url parts joined by dots. The header names the algorithm and key id (alg, kid), the payload holds claims (facts about the user and the token: iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti, plus your own), and the signature covers header.payload. Any service holding the verification key checks it with no call to the issuer. The payload is only encoded, not encrypted: anyone holding the token can read it, so no secrets in it.

howItWorks.title: Verify the right things, in the right order
howItWorks.text: A verifier must (1) pin the expected algorithm from its own configuration instead of trusting the header, (2) pick the key by kid from a trusted set, (3) verify the signature, then (4) check exp and nbf with a small clock skew allowance (30 to 60 seconds, for clocks that differ a little), iss equals the expected issuer, and aud contains this service. Skipping any of these is a known vulnerability, not a style choice.

howItWorks.title: HS256 versus RS256 and ES256, and key rotation
howItWorks.text: HS256 is an HMAC (a hash that needs a secret key) with one shared secret: every verifier can also forge tokens, so it only suits one service or one trust domain. RS256 and ES256 sign with a private key held only by the issuer; verifiers fetch public keys from a JWKS endpoint (a URL that lists public keys, /.well-known/jwks.json). To rotate, publish the new key in the JWKS first, start signing with it (new kid), and remove the old key only after every token it signed has expired.

howItWorks.title: Short access tokens plus rotating refresh tokens
howItWorks.text: Because a JWT cannot be revoked, keep its lifetime to 5 to 15 minutes. A longer-lived refresh token (days to weeks) buys new access tokens from the auth server, which can check its state on each refresh. With rotation every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one; if an old one is ever presented again, someone copied it, so the server revokes the whole token family and forces a new login.

howItWorks.title: Revocation, logout and where to keep the token
howItWorks.text: For urgent revocation you add state back: a deny list of jti (token id) values (kept only until exp), a per-user 'tokens issued before T are invalid' timestamp, or token introspection (RFC 7662) at the cost of a call. In a browser, prefer an HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie that scripts cannot read; localStorage tokens are one XSS (script injection) bug away from theft. Cookies bring CSRF concerns, which SameSite and anti-CSRF tokens address.

pros: Session ids give instant, certain revocation: logout, password change and 'sign out everywhere' take effect on the next request
JWTs are verified with no network call, so many services can authenticate independently and the auth server is off the hot path
Asymmetric signing (RS256, ES256) lets any service verify without being able to mint tokens
Claims such as sub, scope and tenant travel with the request, so downstream services need no user lookup to make a coarse decision
Short access tokens plus refresh rotation bound the damage of a leak and detect token theft
cons: A JWT stays valid until exp: revoking it early needs a deny list or introspection, which reintroduces the lookup you wanted to avoid
A session store is on the critical path of every request: its latency, availability and capacity become yours
A JWT rides on every request: 300 bytes to over 1 KB per call, and big role lists can exceed header limits (often 8 KB at proxies)
Claims go stale: a user demoted at 10:00 still carries 'admin' in a token issued at 09:58
Verification has many sharp edges (algorithm, key selection, audience), and a library default or a missed check silently disables security
whenToUse: Session cookies and a store for a classic first-party web app: revocation and logout matter more than avoiding one Redis hit
Short-lived signed access tokens when many independent services or several organisations must authenticate without sharing a session store
Service-to-service calls where the caller needs a verifiable identity for a few minutes
A token minted by an identity provider (OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect) that your APIs only need to validate
whenNotToUse: A single monolith or a few services behind one gateway: a signed cookie or a session in Redis is simpler, safer and revocable
Using JWTs as long-lived sessions (hours or days) and calling it stateless: you will end up bolting on a deny list that is a session store with extra steps
Stuffing permissions, profile data or anything secret into claims
Rolling your own verification: use a maintained library and pin algorithm, issuer and audience explicitly
pitfalls: Accepting whatever alg the header says: alg=none skips the signature, and handing an RS256 public key to a library that also accepts HS256 lets an attacker sign with the public key as the HMAC secret
No audience check, so a token minted for the low-risk reporting API is accepted by the billing API; likewise no issuer check in multi-tenant setups with shared keys
Treating a 24 hour token as 'logged out' after deleting the cookie: the stolen copy still works, and with no deny list nothing can stop it
Unbounded refresh tokens that are neither rotated nor bound to a device, so a leaked one grants access for months
Comparing signatures with == instead of a constant-time comparison, or using a short or guessable HS256 secret that can be cracked offline
Trusting jku, jwk or x5u header fields, or fetching the JWKS for any kid on demand with no rate limit, so an attacker steers key selection or causes fetch storms

roles.label: Client
roles.description: The user's browser or app, holding the access and refresh tokens.

roles.label: Auth server
roles.description: Authenticates users, issues and rotates tokens, publishes public keys (JWKS).

roles.label: Microservice
roles.description: Verifies the token locally with the issuer's public key and serves the request.

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: Holds a copy of a stolen token.

quiz.question: An API of many microservices accepts 24 hour JWTs and has no deny list. A script injected into the web app steals one user's token at 09:00. The user notices and clicks Log out at 09:30. How long can the thief keep calling the API?
options: Until the token expires, since services verify the signature locally
Until 09:30, since logging out invalidates every token issued to the user
Until the thief's next request, since each service checks the user's session with the auth service
Until the user changes their password, which automatically invalidates all existing tokens
quiz.explanation: A JWT is valid until exp and nothing checks it with a central store. That is the price of local verification, which is why access tokens should be short, 5 to 15 minutes, and revoked via refresh tokens.

quiz.question: A service verifies RS256 tokens with the issuer's public key, but its library takes the algorithm from the token header. An attacker who has the public key crafts a token with alg set to HS256, signed using that public key as the secret, and gets in. What is the best fix?
options: Keep the public key secret so attackers cannot use it as an HMAC secret during verification
Encrypt the token payload so the attacker cannot read the claims or work out the signing algorithm
Shorten the token lifetime to 5 minutes so forged tokens expire quickly
Pin the expected algorithm in the service's own configuration and reject any other
quiz.explanation: Public keys are public by design, and the flaw is trusting the header to choose the algorithm. The verifier must decide the algorithm. Encrypting the payload hides claims but does not stop a forged signature. Shorter lifetimes still let the attacker mint a fresh forged token.

quiz.question: The reporting API and the billing API trust the same issuer and the same signing key. A token issued for the reporting API, validly signed and unexpired, is accepted by billing and used to read invoices. Which check is missing?
options: Verify the token's iat claim is recent, so older tokens cannot be replayed
Check that the aud claim names this service, and reject tokens meant for others
Verify the exp is short enough, so a token for another API expires before it is misused
Rotate the signing key more often, so a token for another API soon stops verifying
quiz.explanation: A signature proves who issued the token, not which service it was meant for. Without an audience check, any token from the issuer works on every service. A short exp or a newer key does not say which API the token is for, and iat only says when it was issued.
